ai.literal: Desire having suffered, to those who grieved, protection except the palmyra stem, there is no strength.
ai.translation: For those who have suffered and grieved in love, there is no strong refuge other than riding the palmyra stem.
ai.modern: காதல் துன்பத்தால் வருந்தியவர்களுக்கு மடல் ஏறுவதைத் தவிர வேறு உறுதியான பாதுகாப்பு இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet captures the desperation of unfulfilled love. The phrase 'காமம் உழந்து வருந்தினார்க்கு' describes those who have struggled and suffered deeply from intense romantic desire. In their extreme distress, their only remaining source of strength and refuge ('ஏமம்', 'வலி') is 'மடல்'. This refers to the ancient Tamil practice where a desperate lover publicly rides a rough horse made of jagged palmyra stems to win their beloved or perish. The speaker asserts that when love brings unbearable pain, this drastic public declaration is the only strong recourse left.

ai.literal: Not-enduring body-and soul-and palmyra-stem will-mount, shame having-removed having-weighed.
ai.translation: Having weighed the pain, my body and soul can endure no more; they will cast aside reserve and ride the palm-stem horse.
ai.modern: துன்பத்தை அளவிட்டுப் பார்த்து, அதனைத் தாங்க முடியாத என் உடம்பும் உயிரும் நாணத்தை நீக்கிவிட்டு மடல் ஏறத் துணிகின்றன.
ai.explanation: The speaker expresses the extreme agony of unfulfilled love, stating that their body and soul can no longer bear the suffering. The word 'நிறுத்து' indicates having weighed this unbearable pain against their natural sense of shame, leading to the decision to abandon reserve. They resolve to ride the 'maṭal' (a horse made of rough palmyra stems), a traditional extreme public declaration of love meant to force the union.

ai.literal: With modesty, good manliness formerly I possessed; today I possess the palmyra stem mounted by those who are infatuated.
ai.translation: I once possessed modesty and excellent manly fortitude. Today, I possess only the palmyra-stem chariot ridden by the infatuated.
ai.modern: முன்பு நான் நாணமும் சிறந்த ஆண்மையும் உடையவனாக இருந்தேன். ஆனால் இன்று காதல் கொண்டவர்கள் ஏறும் மடலையே உடையவனாக இருக்கிறேன்.
ai.explanation: The speaker contrasts his dignified past with his desperate present state caused by intense love. Formerly, he possessed modesty and manly fortitude, which kept his emotions in check. Now, overwhelmed by infatuation, he has lost those virtues and possesses only the palmyra stem. This refers to the ancient Tamil practice of riding a rough chariot made of jagged palmyra stems to publicly declare unrequited love, showing a complete abandonment of shame.

ai.literal: Desire's fierce flood will sweep away indeed, with modesty, the raft called good manliness.
ai.translation: The fierce flood of desire will sweep away the raft of my good fortitude, along with my modesty.
ai.modern: காமம் என்னும் கடுமையான வெள்ளம், நாணம் என்பதோடு நல்ல ஆண்மை என்று சொல்லப்படும் தெப்பத்தையும் அடித்துச் சென்றுவிடும்.
ai.explanation: The speaker compares his overwhelming desire to a fierce, rushing flood. He feels that this flood is too strong to resist and will completely sweep away his sense of modesty. Along with it, the protective raft of his manly fortitude will also be lost. The imagery of the raft emphasizes how fragile his self-control is against the powerful current of love.

ai.translation: The girl wearing a garland and small bracelets has given me the sorrow of riding the palmyra stem and suffering in the evening.
ai.modern: மாலையும் சிறிய வளையல்களும் அணிந்தவள், பனைமடலூர்தலோடு மாலைப் பொழுதில் நான் அனுபவிக்கும் துன்பத்தையும் எனக்குத் தந்தாள்.
ai.explanation: The speaker expresses his intense love and suffering. He says that the young woman, adorned with a garland and small bracelets, is the cause of his current state. Because of her, he is forced to endure the public shame of riding the palmyra stem (maṭal) and the intense sorrow that evening brings to separated lovers. The combination of 'maṭal' and 'evening' highlights the peak of his unbearable agony.

ai.literal: Palmyra chariot riding, even at midnight I will think of, surely; closing they do not agree, for the simple girl, my eyes.
ai.translation: My eyes refuse to close in sleep for the sake of this simple girl. Surely, even at midnight, I think of riding the palmyra chariot.
ai.modern: இந்தப் பேதைப் பெண்ணின் நினைவால் என் கண்கள் மூட மறுக்கின்றன; அதனால் நள்ளிரவிலும் நான் மடல் ஏறுவதைப் பற்றியே உறுதியாக நினைக்கிறேன்.
ai.explanation: The speaker is a lover suffering from intense longing, expressing his desperation. He states that his eyes refuse to close in sleep ('படல் ஒல்லா') because of his love for the simple girl ('பேதை'). Kept awake by this torment even in the dead of night ('யாமத்தும்'), he contemplates riding the 'madal' ('மடல் ஊர்தல்'). Riding the madal is an extreme ancient Tamil custom where a frustrated lover publicly rides a rough chariot of palmyra stems to win his love. The particle 'மன்ற' emphasizes his absolute certainty and resolve in this desperate act.

Therefore, there is nothing greater than the dignity and modesty of a woman.

ai.literal: firmness - rare persons - indeed - pitiable persons - not saying - passion - secret - having crossed - public assembly - will appear
ai.translation: Passion does not care that one's self-control is hard-won or that one's state is pitiable. It breaks out of secrecy and exposes itself in the public square.
ai.modern: 'இவர்கள் மன உறுதி மிக்கவர்கள், மிகவும் பரிதாபத்திற்கு உரியவர்கள்' என்று பார்க்காமல், காமம் ரகசிய எல்லையைத் தாண்டி பொது மன்றத்தில் வெளிப்பட்டு விடும்.
ai.explanation: The speaker expresses how overwhelming love cannot be hidden. Passion is personified as a relentless force that does not pity the lover's suffering ('அளியர்') or respect their hard-won self-control ('நிறை அரியர்'). Instead of remaining a private secret ('மறை'), it breaks all boundaries ('இறந்து') and exposes the lover's feelings to the entire public assembly ('மன்று'). This highlights the uncontrollable and public nature of intense romantic longing.

ai.literal: Thinking indeed 'all people know not', my passion in the street wanders being bewildered.
ai.translation: Thinking that no one knows about it, my passion wanders bewildered in the public street.
ai.modern: என் காதல், 'எல்லாரும் இதை அறியமாட்டார்கள்' என்று நினைத்துக்கொண்டு, மயங்கித் தெருவிலே சுழன்று திரிகிறது.
ai.explanation: The speaker's secret love has grown so intense that it can no longer be hidden. The passion itself is personified as being bewildered ('மருண்டு'), foolishly thinking that the public is unaware of it ('அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றே'), while it openly exposes itself by wandering in the streets. The word 'மறுகு' is used beautifully in two senses: as a noun meaning 'street' ('மறுகின்') and as a verb meaning 'to whirl or wander in distress' ('மறுகும்').

ai.literal: we with eyes to see they laugh those without understanding, we experienced they not experiencing because
ai.translation: Those without understanding laugh right before my eyes, because they have not suffered what I have suffered.
ai.modern: நான் பட்ட துன்பத்தை அவர்கள் படாத காரணத்தால், அறிவில்லாதவர்கள் என் கண்ணெதிரிலேயே என்னைப் பார்த்துச் சிரிக்கிறார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The speaker laments the mockery of the townspeople who do not understand the torment of love. The phrase 'யாம் கண்ணின் காண' means they laugh right in front of the speaker's eyes, showing a complete lack of empathy. They are called 'அறிவில்லார்' (those without understanding) because they judge without knowing the speaker's plight. The reason for their mockery is 'யாம் பட்ட தாம் படா ஆறு'—they have simply not experienced the suffering that the speaker is enduring. The poetic 'யாம்' (we) is used here by the speaker to refer to themselves.
